candidates.summary: The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules: \begin{enumerate} \item Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\). \item If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\). \item If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\). \item No string is a well-formed formula unless it is obtained by finitely many applications of the previous clauses. \

candidates.summary: Let $\Sigma=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar})$ be a first-order signature. The \emph{arity function} is the map \[   \operatorname{ar}:\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0} \] that assigns to each function or relation symbol the number of arguments it requires. When constants are treated as $0$-ary function symbols, the codomain is enlarged to include $0$.

For a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), a \emph{constant symbol} is a non-logical symbol of arity \(0\). A constant symbol may occur as a term without taking input terms.

For a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), an \(n\)-ary \emph{function symbol} is a non-logical symbol of arity \(n\geq 1\). If \(f\) has arity \(n\), then it forms terms by the pattern \[ f(t_1,\ldots,t_n). \]

A \emph{relation symbol}, or predicate symbol, is a non-logical symbol $R\in\mathcal{R}$ whose assigned arity determines how many terms it must take as inputs. If $\operatorname{ar}(R)=n$, then $R$ is an $n$-ary formula constructor: it takes exactly $n$ terms and produces an atomic formula, hence something with a truth value rather than an object.

For a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), an \(n\)-ary \emph{predicate symbol} is a non-logical symbol of arity \(n\geq 1\). If \(P\) has arity \(n\), then it forms atomic formulas by the pattern \[ P(t_1,\ldots,t_n). \]

A \emph{constant symbol} is a non-logical symbol that behaves syntactically as a $0$-ary function symbol. In the streamlined convention where constants are included among function symbols, this is the condition \[   \operatorname{Constant}(c)   \iff c\in\mathcal{F}\text{ and }\operatorname{ar}(c)=0. \] Because its arity is $0$, the symbol $c$ is already a well-formed term and takes no input terms.

A \emph{function symbol} is a non-logical symbol $f\in\mathcal{F}$ whose assigned arity determines how many terms it must take as inputs. If $\operatorname{ar}(f)=n$, then $f$ is an $n$-ary term constructor: it takes exactly $n$ terms and produces a new term, not a truth value.

candidates.summary: The depth of a formula \(\varphi\), denoted \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)\), is defined recursively: \begin{enumerate} \item if \(\varphi\) is atomic, then \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=0\); \item if \(\varphi=\neg\psi\), then \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=\operatorname{depth}(\psi)+1\); \item if \(\varphi=(\psi\circ\chi)\), then \[ \operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=\max\{\operatorname{depth}(\psi),\operatorname{depth}(\chi)\}+1. \] \end{enumerate}
